title: Meditation as practice

lines: A BOY UNDER A ROSE-APPLE TREE.
THE MEMORY THAT CHANGED THE PATH.
cards: A man has been starving himself in the forest for a long time. In the story, he eats so little that when he touches his belly he can feel his spine. He holds his breath until there's a roaring in his ears.
Nothing he's looking for comes. Then, worn down to almost nothing, he remembers an afternoon from when he was a small boy. His father was at work in the fields.

The boy sat in the cool shade of a rose-apple tree, and his mind went quiet and glad all by itself. The man is the future Buddha, and you met that tree early on the path. The memory changes his whole path.

teach.h: THE MEMORY OF THE ROSE-APPLE TREE.
teach.b: In the Middle Length Discourses, the Buddha tells this himself.

teach.h: NO NEED TO FEAR THAT CALM.
teach.b: Remembering the rose-apple tree, he asks: could that be the way to awakening? And he answers: that is the way.

Then he asks why he should be afraid of a happiness that has nothing to do with sense pleasures or unwholesome things. He decides not to be afraid of it. He eats a little rice, gets his strength back, and sits.
So meditation here doesn't start with force. It starts with a calm he already knew, and a willingness to trust it. The Pali word for those deep absorptions is jhana.
In Sanskrit it's dhyana, and in the Mahayana list of perfections dhyana is the fifth: meditative steadiness, a mind that can stay.

Tradition says the name of the Chan school in China, Zen in Japan, comes from this same word. The second side is steady, daily. At the close of one teaching in the Middle Length Discourses, the Buddha puts it plainly.

teach.h: THE ROOTS OF TREES: SIT THERE.
teach.b: Here are the roots of trees, here are empty huts. Meditate. Don't be careless, or you'll regret it later.
He points at an ordinary place and says, sit there. The perfection isn't one great sitting. It's the habit of sitting, the way a path through a field is made by walking it every day.
A long sitting now and then is good. A short one every day wears the path in.

how: Buddhists in many schools keep a daily sitting practice at home or in a temple, often at the same time each day; in the Mahayana list of six perfections, meditation (dhyana) is the fifth.

o: one long retreat you do once to reach awakening
a steady mind, built by sitting a little every day
a trance you reach by forcing out every thought

games.q: meditation as practice: tap the pairs.
p: where the boy's mind went quiet
the Pali word for deep absorption
where the Buddha says to sit

s: the Buddha found the way by starving himself harder
the starving brought nothing; a childhood memory of calm turned him back to eating and sitting.
the Buddha decided not to fear the happiness of meditation
he asks why he should fear a happiness apart from sense pleasures, and decides not to.
the perfection of meditation is one great sitting
the Buddha says: here are the roots of trees, sit. the perfection is a daily habit.

games.q: you're the future Buddha, worn thin by fasting. you remember a quiet afternoon in the shade as a boy. what do you do?
o: trust that calm, eat a little and sit.
give up the search and go home.
games.why: he says to himself, that is the way, decides not to fear that happiness, eats some rice and sits.

practice: Find your own patch of shade: sit easy and upright, hands resting, and let the breath come and go without managing it.
When the mind wanders, and it will, notice where it went and come back, the way the Buddha came back to a quiet afternoon. No need to force anything.

wordCard.voice: Meditation as practice. Dhyana, the fifth perfection: a steady mind, built by sitting a little every day. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit dhyana (Pali jhana): meditative absorption; the fifth of the six perfections in the Mahayana list.

carryVoice: Your line: the fifth perfection. A bench, a parked car or a quiet stair can be the root of a tree. Until tomorrow.
